items.label: f04-receipt-needs-outbox
items.front: The confirmation box claims receipts and delivery links 'were issued' though no code sends anything (src/App.tsx:406-414). When orders become real, how should the receipt email leave the system?
items.back: Through an outbox: persist the intent-to-send in the same transaction as the order, have a worker deliver it with retry and dedupe, and only report success from delivery state - never assert side effects from render code.

items.label: f03-admin-no-authz
items.front: The Admin view (KYC, chargebacks, payout reserves) renders whenever local state holds the admin view key (src/App.tsx:165). What is missing before this surface can face users?
items.back: Authentication and authorization end to end: sessions, an admin role separate from creator, server-enforced route and API guards, IDs from params treated as untrusted, and cross-role rejection tests - a TypeScript union over view names is not access control.

items.label: f01-unsafe-cart-hydration
items.front: Cart hydration runs JSON.parse on localStorage inside a useState initializer, with a blind as-string[] cast and no try/catch (src/App.tsx:53-56). Risk and fix?
items.back: One corrupt value crashes the whole app at startup, and valid-but-wrong JSON sails past the cast into state. Fix: a safe parser that catches, validates an array of known product ids, logs invalid input, and falls back to a default cart.

items.label: f02-float-money-client-math
items.front: Prices are floating-point numbers (src/types.ts:14) and subtotal/discount/tax/total are computed in the browser (src/App.tsx:344-348). What must change before real payments?
items.back: Represent money as integer cents with an explicit currency, make the server the price authority that recomputes every total from ids, and source tax from a jurisdiction-aware service instead of a hardcoded 8.25% client-side multiplier.

items.prompt: After clicking Pay now, the UI shows a confirmed order number and says licenses, receipts and delivery links were issued. What is actually true?

choices.text: Nothing was issued: it is hardcoded JSX, and the order number is a literal
Licensing is mocked: the order number is generated fresh for each purchase
An order record was saved and appended to localStorage next to the cart ids
A receipt email was queued: it sends in the background, but delivery is not awaited

choices: Nothing was issued: it is hardcoded JSX, and the order number is a literal
Licensing is mocked: the order number is generated fresh for each purchase
An order record was saved and appended to localStorage next to the cart ids
A receipt email was queued: it sends in the background, but delivery is not awaited

items.explanation: The confirmation box is hardcoded JSX behind a boolean. 'Order BG-98241 confirmed' is literal text, as is the 'Fraud scoring, tax evidence, and license provisioning are enabled' trust row - the register files both under mock operational claims mistaken as real.

items.prompt: filteredProducts is recomputed from products and query on every render instead of living in its own useState. What bug class does that choice remove?

choices.text: StrictMode corruption: double-invoked effects overwrite the stored list
Stale closures that capture an old query inside the event handlers
Infinite render loops: a state setter called during render re-renders forever
Stale-copy drift: a stored filtered list could disagree with its sources

choices: StrictMode corruption: double-invoked effects overwrite the stored list
Stale closures that capture an old query inside the event handlers
Infinite render loops: a state setter called during render re-renders forever
Stale-copy drift: a stored filtered list could disagree with its sources

items.explanation: A stored filtered list could disagree with products or query whenever some update path forgets to refresh it. The guide's invariant: products stay the single source of product facts and the cart stores only ids - 'If filtering moved into a mutation handler, new query paths could forget it.'

items.prompt: A buyer clicks 'Add to cart' on a product that is already in the cart. What changes?

choices.text: The line item's quantity increments by one, and the total updates with it
The id list is unchanged, but the product is selected and checkout resets
No state changes: the handler returns early before its state setters run
A second copy of the id is appended, so the product would be charged twice

choices: The line item's quantity increments by one, and the total updates with it
The id list is unchanged, but the product is selected and checkout resets
No state changes: the handler returns early before its state setters run
A second copy of the id is appended, so the product would be charged twice

items.explanation: An includes guard keeps the id list untouched, but checkoutComplete resets to false: setCartIds keeps `current` when current.includes(product.id), while the other two setters still run - and there is no quantity concept at all; the cart is a set of ids.

items.prompt: A buyer types ' build20 ' - lowercase, padded with spaces - into the discount field. Does the discount apply?

choices.text: Not at first; it applies on a second render, since promo state is async
Yes: the lookup trims and uppercases the input before comparing
No: the whitespace fails the field's HTML validation before state updates
No: the comparison is exact and case-sensitive against the stored code

choices: Not at first; it applies on a second render, since promo state is async
Yes: the lookup trims and uppercases the input before comparing
No: the whitespace fails the field's HTML validation before state updates
No: the comparison is exact and case-sensitive against the stored code

items.explanation: `discounts.find((d) => d.code === promo.trim().toUpperCase())` normalizes the input - while expiry and redemption bounds are still ignored entirely.

items.prompt: The reliability guide worries about 'Pay now' being pressed twice, yet in today's code a double click causes no harm. Why?

choices.text: It only sets a local checkoutComplete flag, and no request exists to duplicate
An idempotency key derived from the order id makes the second click a no-op
The button disables itself after the first click and stays off until the cart changes
React batches both clicks into one state update, so the handler runs once

choices: It only sets a local checkoutComplete flag, and no request exists to duplicate
An idempotency key derived from the order id makes the second click a no-op
The button disables itself after the first click and stays off until the cart changes
React batches both clicks into one state update, so the handler runs once

items.explanation: onComplete is () => setCheckoutComplete(true) - there is no request anywhere that could create a duplicate order. The guide's point: the moment a real payment call lands here, it needs idempotency keys and server-side order state.

items.prompt: The Orders table resolves each row's product with a products.find inside orders.map. With 50,000 orders and 5,000 products, what is the cost shape and the standard fix?

choices.text: O(orders x products); build a Map keyed by product id once, then look up
Sort both arrays first so that find becomes O(log n), which is enough
O(orders + products); that is already linear, so no change is needed
React keys are the real bottleneck, so windowing the table is the fix

choices: O(orders x products); build a Map keyed by product id once, then look up
Sort both arrays first so that find becomes O(log n), which is enough
O(orders + products); that is already linear, so no change is needed
React keys are the real bottleneck, so windowing the table is the fix

items.explanation: A linear find per mapped row is a quadratic nested-loop join - harmless at seed-data size, flagged by the register as a scaling risk; a keyed lookup map (constant-time per row) or a backend join removes it.

items.prompt: Checkout computes subtotal, discount, tax (hardcoded 8.25%) and total entirely in the browser. If payments were wired to this code unchanged, what is the headline risk?

choices.text: The tax rate is wrong for international buyers alone, so US launches are fine
Floating-point drift leaves totals off by a cent at most, which is acceptable
The client controls the amounts, so tampered totals get charged as-is
Concurrent React renders could drop an applied discount from the final total

choices: The tax rate is wrong for international buyers alone, so US launches are fine
Floating-point drift leaves totals off by a cent at most, which is acceptable
The client controls the amounts, so tampered totals get charged as-is
Concurrent React renders could drop an applied discount from the final total

items.explanation: A tampered subtotal or discount would be charged as-is - prices need server-side authority. The register rates client checkout math High impact / High likelihood once payments exist: totals must be recomputed server-side and the single hardcoded jurisdiction rate replaced by a tax service - US sales tax already varies by state.

choices.text: The cart quietly falls back to the seeded default holding the first product
React catches the parse error, then renders the storefront with an empty cart
The corrupt entry is filtered out by the type predicate inside cartProducts
JSON.parse throws in the useState initializer, crashing the app before it renders

React catches the parse error, then renders the storefront with an empty cart
The corrupt entry is filtered out by the type predicate inside cartProducts
JSON.parse throws in the useState initializer, crashing the app before it renders

items.explanation: The initializer runs `stored ? (JSON.parse(stored) as string[]) : ...` with no try/catch; the risk register's suggested fix is a safe parser with a malformed-localStorage test.

items.prompt: A saved cart contains the id of a product that has since been removed from the catalog. What does the buyer see, and what remains in localStorage?

choices.text: The initializer prunes unknown ids, so storage is cleaned up
The item vanishes from the cart, but its id stays in storage
Rendering crashes, because find returns undefined in the map
The cart shows a placeholder row for the unavailable product

choices: The initializer prunes unknown ids, so storage is cleaned up
The item vanishes from the cart, but its id stays in storage
Rendering crashes, because find returns undefined in the map
The cart shows a placeholder row for the unavailable product

items.explanation: cartProducts drops unmatched ids via the filter type predicate, but the persistence effect serializes raw cartIds, so the stale id keeps being written back - the display and the stored cart quietly disagree.

items.prompt: The ProductStatus union gains a new 'Archived' value and a product uses it. The build is green. What happens to that product's status badge?

choices.text: React logs an unknown-className warning and drops the class for the new value
The row fails to render, because the new status is missing from the pill map
The generic .pill fallback rule styles it exactly the same as a Draft badge
Class 'pill archived' gets the neutral .pill rule and no status colour

choices: React logs an unknown-className warning and drops the class for the new value
The row fails to render, because the new status is missing from the pill map
The generic .pill fallback rule styles it exactly the same as a Draft badge
Class 'pill archived' gets the neutral .pill rule and no status colour

items.explanation: The badge silently loses its status colour: the generic .pill rule (beige #eee8db) still applies, but no .pill.archived rule exists. (Item corrected in the rebalance-2 fix pass: the key used to say the badge loses all styling.) Class names are derived from data at runtime (`pill ${status.toLowerCase()}`), and style.css only knows live/review/paused/draft - the compiler cannot see the gap, which is why the register wants explicit maps and fallbacks.

items.prompt: What stands between a curious storefront visitor and the Admin view with its KYC, chargeback and payout-reserve panels?

choices.text: The ViewKey union type excludes 'admin' from the storefront production build
A signed session cookie: the admin screen is server-rendered behind it
A role check: buyer sessions never see the admin entries, so they cannot open it
Only local UI state: setting the view key renders Admin, with no auth at all

A signed session cookie: the admin screen is server-rendered behind it
A role check: buyer sessions never see the admin entries, so they cannot open it
Only local UI state: setting the view key renders Admin, with no auth at all

items.explanation: The main switch is plain conditional rendering on a useState value - no auth, role or session exists anywhere. The guide is explicit that ViewKey prevents typoed view names, not unauthorized access.

items.prompt: localStorage holds the string {"id":1} - valid JSON, wrong shape. Where does this actually blow up?

choices.text: Nowhere: TypeScript drops values that do not match the annotation at runtime
In the persistence effect, which refuses to serialize a value that is not an array
Not at the parse: the cast lets the object through, and cartIds.map then throws
At JSON.parse, which rejects a top-level JSON value, as it is not an array

choices: Nowhere: TypeScript drops values that do not match the annotation at runtime
In the persistence effect, which refuses to serialize a value that is not an array
Not at the parse: the cast lets the object through, and cartIds.map then throws
At JSON.parse, which rejects a top-level JSON value, as it is not an array

items.explanation: A type assertion is not runtime validation (the guide's 'Type assertion after parse' row): the as-string[] assertion accepts the object, it lands in state untouched, and the first derive that calls `.map` on it is the first call that fails.
